content: The development of these recommendations was made possible through the contributions of the Guideline Development Group, the scientists who conducted systematic reviews, and the external peer reviewers. Professor K. Srinath chaired the meetings, with support from the deputy chair, Professor Nizal Sarrafzadegan. The WHO Steering Group included members from various departments and regional offices, such as Bernadette Cappello (Department of Essential Medicines and Products), Neerja Chowdhury (Department of Mental Health), and Gampo Dorji (Regional Office for South-East Asia). Other notable contributors included Jill Farrington (Regional Office for Europe), Taskeen Khan (Department of Noncommunicable Diseases), Pedro Orduñez (Pan American Health Organization/Regional Office of the Americas), Steven Shongwe (Regional Office for Africa), Slim Slama (Regional Office for the Eastern Mediterranean), Cherian Varghese (Department of Noncommunicable Diseases), Marco Vitoria (Department of HIV/AIDS), and Temo Waqanivalu (Department of Noncommunicable Diseases). The Guideline Development Group comprised experts from diverse regions and specialties. For example, Dr. Shrish Acharya, a consultant physician and head of internal medicine in Fiji, contributed expertise in clinical practice guideline development. Dr. Akram Al-Makki, a nephrologist and director of graduate medical education in the USA, provided insights into hypertension management in disaster settings and the pharmacology of antihypertensive medications. Dr. Hind Mamoun Beheiry, an associate professor of physiology and dean of the Faculty of Nursing Sciences in Sudan, focused on nursing, hypertension care in low-resource settings, and community-level prevention. Other contributors included Beatriz Champagne, who emphasized advocacy and policy change in Latin America, and Dr. Kenneth Connell, a clinical pharmacologist from Barbados, who specialized in hypertension and ethnicity. Dr. Marie Therese Cooney, a geriatrician from Ireland, contributed expertise in cardiovascular risk estimation and multimorbidity. Dr. Donald DiPette, a professor of clinical pharmacology in the USA, provided insights into hypertension pathophysiology and health policy. Dr. Nnenna Ezeigwe, a public health physician from Nigeria, focused on policy-making and program implementation for noncommunicable diseases. Dr. Tom Gaziano, an associate professor at Harvard Medical School, contributed expertise in global health policy, cost-effectiveness, and hypertension treatment implementation. Dr. Agaba Gidio, an endocrinologist from Uganda, focused on hypertension in diabetic patients. Dr. Vilma Irazola, a researcher from Argentina, emphasized implementation science and cardiovascular health. Dr. Patricio Lopez Jaramillo, an endocrinologist from Colombia, contributed expertise in clinical hypertension management and research. Dr. Unaib Khan, a family medicine specialist from Pakistan, focused on educational programs for primary care physicians and workplace wellness. Dr. Vindya Kumarapeli, a public health expert from Sri Lanka, emphasized access to hypertension care in low-resource settings. Dr. Andrew Moran, a hypertension control director in the USA, contributed expertise in primary care and health economics. Dr. Margaret Mswema Silwimba, a clinical pharmacist from Zambia, focused on hypertension pharmaceuticals and pharmacy education. Dr. Brian Rayner, an emeritus professor from South Africa, specialized in resistant hypertension and diabetic kidney disease. Dr. K. Srinath Reddy, president of the Public Health Foundation of India, contributed expertise in cardiology, epidemiology, and health systems. Dr. Nizal Sarrafzadegan, a distinguished professor of cardiology from Iran, focused on noncommunicable disease prevention and global health. Dr. Apichard Sukonthasarn, a cardiac specialist from Thailand, emphasized cardiovascular disease prevention and hypertension management. Dr. Paul Whelton, a professor at Tulane University, contributed expertise in cardiovascular and renal disease prevention. Dr. Jing Yu, a cardiologist from China, focused on hypertension complications and access to care in low-resource settings. The guideline development process was coordinated by the WHO Department of Noncommunicable Diseases, with the first draft written by Taskeen Khan. The drafts were reviewed by the Guideline Development Group and the External Review Group, and revisions were made accordingly. The process adhered to WHO's Compliance, Risk Management, and Ethics (CRE) policy, with all members completing Declaration of Interest forms. No conflicts of interest were deemed significant enough to affect the objectivity of the recommendations. However, one member was removed from further participation after accepting a temporary appointment at WHO. The guideline also included a systematic review of treatment outcomes relevant to hypertension care. Outcomes were rated on a scale of importance, with critical outcomes including stroke, myocardial infarction, cardiovascular death, heart failure, and end-stage renal disease.
